accident_report:
Vehicle initialization
On a one-way three-lane uphill straight road, the pavement is wet due to persistent rain under adverse weather conditions, reducing tire-road friction. V1 is traveling in lane 2 at 70 km/h, maintaining a nominally safe following distance behind V2, which is ahead in the same lane at 68 km/h. V3 is in lane 1 (rightmost lane) slightly behind V1, traveling at 72 km/h, intending to overtake. V4 is further ahead in lane 2 at 65 km/h, acting as a slower-moving vehicle influencing the flow. The wide shoulder on the right side is clear but damp. All vehicles are maintaining coordinated speeds with relatively small speed differences due to traffic flow conditions.

Scene development
As the vehicles progress uphill, the gradient slightly reduces engine efficiency, causing V4 to decelerate gradually from 65 km/h to 58 km/h. This speed reduction propagates backward: V2 begins to slow from 68 km/h to 60 km/h to maintain safe following distance, and V1 correspondingly reduces speed from 70 km/h to 62 km/h, still keeping a controlled gap. Meanwhile, V3 in lane 1 attempts to overtake V1 by increasing speed slightly to 75 km/h, taking advantage of the speed coordination and open adjacent lane.

However, due to the wet and slippery road surface combined with reduced visibility from the adverse weather, V3 misjudges the relative speed and position of V2 and V1. As V3 draws level with V1, V2 suddenly applies moderate braking (down to 50 km/h) because the uphill resistance causes V4 ahead to slow more sharply than expected. This creates a compression effect in lane 2.

V1 reacts by braking more firmly, reducing speed from 62 km/h to 48 km/h. At this moment, V3, now slightly ahead of V1 but still partially overlapping, attempts an illegal evasive maneuver by cutting into lane 2 with insufficient lateral clearance, aiming to avoid getting boxed in behind slowing traffic. The maneuver is unstable due to the slippery surface; V3’s lateral movement is slower and less controlled than intended.

The partial lane intrusion by V3 forces V1 to brake harder, dropping speed further to 40 km/h, while V2 ahead continues at approximately 50 km/h. The reduced friction prevents V1 from achieving the desired deceleration smoothly, increasing stopping distance. The combined effects of uphill resistance, wet road, and tight spacing lead to rapid gap closure between V1 and V2.

Result
The first collision occurs when V1 rear-ends V2 in lane 2 at approximately 35 km/h relative speed. The crash is directly caused by the chain reaction of uphill-induced deceleration, slippery road conditions reducing braking efficiency, and V3’s illegal evasive lane change that forced V1 into excessive braking under constrained spacing.
